fixes.explanation: Yes, he's the one. The chief cupbearer speaks up to Pharaoh with “Today I recall my failures.” (Genesis 41:9). Then he tells the king about a young Hebrew who interpreted his dream and the chief baker's dream (Genesis 41:12). I know a thing or two about being remembered late. I spent years in the back of a junk drawer before anybody came looking.

It goes the other way, friend. The text doesn't have the thin cows running back into the river or getting scared of anybody. It says the sickly, thin cows “…devoured the seven sleek, well-fed cows.” (Genesis 41:4). The skinny ones are the ones doing the devouring.

The text says it plainly: “In the morning his spirit was troubled…” (Genesis 41:8). Pharaoh, king of Egypt, dreamed of thin cows devouring well-fed cows, then fell back asleep and dreamed of thin heads of grain swallowing plump ones (Genesis 41:4-7). I'd be rattled too. He doesn't shrug it off. He summons the magicians and wise men of Egypt.

Joyful would mean Pharaoh, king of Egypt, woke up humming. Genesis 41:8 says “In the morning his spirit was troubled…” I bet cows eating cows would do that to a person. In that same verse, he summons the magicians and wise men of Egypt.

Rested sounds nice, and Pharaoh, king of Egypt, did fall back asleep between the dreams (Genesis 41:5). But the text says “In the morning his spirit was troubled…” (Genesis 41:8). Troubled and rested don't go together. So he summons the magicians and wise men to explain the dreams.

That's the crowd. Genesis 41:8 says Pharaoh, king of Egypt, “…summoned all the magicians and wise men of Egypt.” When his spirit is troubled, he doesn't text one guy. He calls the whole group chat. And still, the verse says no one could interpret the dreams for him.

The captain of the guard does show up later in the passage. The cupbearer says the young Hebrew was a servant of the captain of the guard (Genesis 41:12). But the ones Pharaoh, king of Egypt, summons are “…all the magicians and wise men of Egypt.” (Genesis 41:8). Different crowd.

The cupbearer says it himself: “I was restored to my position…” (Genesis 41:13). That's just what the young Hebrew had interpreted for him. He's back in his old position with Pharaoh, king of Egypt. That's a job comeback if I ever heard one.

The captain of the guard is the man who had the cupbearer and the chief baker in custody (Genesis 41:10). The cupbearer doesn't take his job. The cupbearer says, “I was restored to my position…” (Genesis 41:13). He goes back to the work he had before.

It does happen, friend. After the cupbearer speaks, “…Pharaoh sent for Joseph, who was quickly brought out of the dungeon.” (Genesis 41:14). Joseph is the young Hebrew the cupbearer described. Quickly is the word the text uses, and I think Joseph didn't mind the rush.

Joseph has been in the dungeon, so I get why that came to mind. But his reply doesn't ask for anything. He tells Pharaoh, king of Egypt, “I myself cannot do it, but God will give Pharaoh a sound answer” (Genesis 41:16). His reply points to God.

Pharaoh, king of Egypt, says the opposite. After the thin cows devoured the well-fed ones, “…no one could tell that they had done so; their appearance was as ugly as it had been before.” (Genesis 41:21). Not one bit of difference. I think that's exactly why Pharaoh stresses it to Joseph, the young Hebrew.

Egypt is the stage, not the one acting. Joseph says, “God has revealed to Pharaoh what He is about to do.” (Genesis 41:25). Pharaoh, king of Egypt, is the one who gets the heads-up. The stage never gets handed the script.

That's right. Joseph says the abundance “…will be forgotten…” and “…will not be remembered…” once the famine arrives (Genesis 41:30-31). He says the famine will be that severe. It's like a great weekend you forget the second your car breaks down on the way home.

Remembering it longer is a sensible guess, and Pharaoh's spirit was troubled in the morning (Genesis 41:8). But Joseph gives a different reason. He says it was given in two versions because “…the matter has been decreed by God, and He will carry it out shortly.” (Genesis 41:32). He doesn't mention Pharaoh's memory.

The magicians did miss it, since the text says no one could interpret the dreams for Pharaoh (Genesis 41:8). But Joseph's reason has nothing to do with them. He says it was given in two versions because “…the matter has been decreed by God, and He will carry it out shortly.” (Genesis 41:32).

Joseph says, “This food will be a reserve for the land during the seven years of famine to come upon the land of Egypt.” (Genesis 41:36). That's his plan: collect the excess food in the good years and lay up grain in the cities (Genesis 41:35). Save now, so the lean years don't catch the land empty-handed.
